{{Short description|Austrian physicist (born 1969)}}
{{COI|date=May 2026}}
{{TOC right}}
'''Stefan Thurner''' (born 1969) is an Austrian physicist and complexity scientist. He heads the Section for Science of Complex Systems at the [[Medical University of Vienna]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Wien |first=Medizinischen Universität |title=Researcher of the MedUni Vienna |url=https://www.meduniwien.ac.at//web/forschung/researcher-profiles/researcher-profiles/detail/ |access-date=2026-03-06 |website=Medizinischen Universität Wien |language=de}}</ref> and is a co-founder and the president of the [[Complexity Science Hub]] (CSH).<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Complexity Science Hub * Stefan Thurner |url=https://csh.ac.at/stefan-thurner/ |access-date=2026-03-06 |language=en-US}}</ref> Thurner also serves as an external professor at the [[Santa Fe Institute]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stefan Thurner {{!}} Santa Fe Institute |url=https://www.santafe.edu//people/profile/stefan-thurner |access-date=2026-03-06 |website=www.santafe.edu |language=en}}</ref>

His research focuses on extending statistical mechanics to networked [[complex system]]s out of equilibrium, with applications to the dynamics and [[phase transition]]s of social, biological, and economic systems. Notable contributions include a theory for systems out-of-equilibrium, stress-testing of [[Health system|healthcare systems]], [[agent-based model]]ling of [[systemic risk]] in [[supply chain]]s and [[financial network]]s, and the quantification of [[Resilience (mathematics)|resilience]]. He authored ''Introduction to the Theory of Complex Systems'', a textbook on complex systems.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last1=Thurner |first1=Stefan |url=https://academic.oup.com/book/25504 |title=Introduction to the Theory of Complex Systems |last2=Klimek |first2=Peter |last3=Hanel |first3=Rudolf |date=2018-11-22 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-882193-9 |volume=1 |language=en |doi=10.1093/oso/9780198821939.001.0001}}</ref>

Thurner has received awards including Austrian Scientist of the Year 2017 <ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Komplexitätsforscher Thurner zum Wissenschafter des Jahres gewählt |url=https://www.derstandard.at/story/2000071634414/komplexitaetsforscher-zum-wissenschafter-des-jahres-gewaehlt |access-date=2026-03-06 |website=DER STANDARD |language=de-AT}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=WissenschafterIn des Jahres {{!}} |url=https://www.wissenschaftsjournalisten.at/wissenschafter-des-jahres/ |access-date=2026-03-06 |language=de}}</ref> and the Paul Watzlawick Ring of Honor (2021).<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=Peter Klimek und Stefan Thurner (2021) – Paul Watzlawick Ehrenring |url=https://watzlawickehrenring.at/peter-klimek-und-stefan-thurner-2021 |access-date=2026-03-06 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Career ==

===Early life and education===
Thurner was born in [[1969]] in [[Innsbruck]], Austria.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-01-08 |title=Komplexitätsforscher Stefan Thurner |url=https://science.orf.at/v2/stories/2888159/ |access-date=2026-03-06 |website=science.ORF.at |language=de}}</ref> He received a PhD in [[theoretical physics]] from [[TU Wien]] and a second PhD in [[economics]] from the [[University of Vienna]]. He completed his [[habilitation]] in theoretical physics at [[TU Wien]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=Talks at NetSI {{!}} Stefan Thurner |url=https://www.networkscienceinstitute.org/talks/stefan-thurner |access-date=2026-03-06 |website=www.networkscienceinstitute.org |language=en}}</ref>

Thurner started his academic career in theoretical particle physics before transitioning to research on [[complex adaptive system]]s, building on mathematical modelling and quantitative methods.<ref name=":7" />

=== Professional career ===
After completing his PhD, Thurner held postdoctoral positions at [[Humboldt University of Berlin]] and [[Boston University]], before joining the [[University of Vienna]] as a faculty member.

From 2001 to 2004, he was Associate Professor at the [[University of Vienna]], studying networks and collective dynamics in biological, social, and economic systems. In 2001, he completed his habilitation in theoretical physics and earned his second PhD in economics, integrating statistical mechanics with economic modelling to study systemic risks and growth patterns.

From 2004 to 2009, as associate professor at the [[Medical University of Vienna]], he expanded his research to [[health]] and medical applications, including network-based analyses of hospital data, disease [[Comorbidity|comorbidities]], and [[Health system|healthcare system]] [[resilience]]. He has served as an external professor at the [[Santa Fe Institute]] since 2007 and was a fellow at [[Institute for Advanced Study at Central European University|Collegium Budapest]] the same year. Since 2009, he has held a full professorship in Science of Complex Systems at the Medical University of Vienna.

In 2016, he co-founded the [[Complexity Science Hub]] (CSH) in [[Vienna]] and became its president.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":1" /> The Complexity Science Hub is an interdisciplinary research center for the study of complex adaptive systems, comprising eleven member institutions and a global network of external faculty.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-12-07 |title=External Faculty * Complexity Science Hub |url=https://csh.ac.at/people/external-faculty/ |access-date=2026-03-06 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-10-30 |title=About Us * Complexity Science Hub |url=https://csh.ac.at/about-us/ |access-date=2026-03-06 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Research ==
Stefan Thurner's research is grounded in [[theoretical physics]] of [[complex system]]s and aims at the quantitative characterization of [[Emergence|emergent]] phenomena in [[Dimension|high-dimensional]], [[Nonlinear system|nonlinear]], and [[Non-equilibrium thermodynamics|non-equilibrium]] systems. Using methods from [[statistical mechanics]], [[network theory]], and [[agent-based model]]ling, his research investigates the structural and dynamical properties of economic, biological, and social systems.

=== Foundations of Complex Systems ===
Thurner has contributed foundational tools for quantifying complexity in non-equilibrium systems, including a derivation of generalized [[entropy]] measures for complex systems from first principles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hanel |first1=R. |last2=Thurner |first2=S. |date=2011-12-01 |title=When do generalized entropies apply? How phase space volume determines entropy |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1209/0295-5075/96/50003 |journal=EPL (Europhysics Letters) |volume=96 |issue=5 |article-number=50003 |doi=10.1209/0295-5075/96/50003 |arxiv=1104.2064 |bibcode=2011EL.....9650003H |issn=0295-5075}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hanel |first1=R. |last2=Thurner |first2=S. |date=2011-01-01 |title=A comprehensive classification of complex statistical systems and an axiomatic derivation of their entropy and distribution functions |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1209/0295-5075/93/20006 |journal=EPL (Europhysics Letters) |volume=93 |issue=2 |article-number=20006 |doi=10.1209/0295-5075/93/20006 |bibcode=2011EL.....9320006H |issn=0295-5075}}</ref> He contributed to the understanding of the statistics of open, driven, out-of-equilibrium systems with the so-called sample space reducing processes that offer an intuitively simple and mathematically tractable explanation of non-Gaussian statistics in complex systems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Corominas-Murtra |first1=Bernat |last2=Hanel |first2=Rudolf |last3=Thurner |first3=Stefan |date=2015-04-28 |title=Understanding scaling through history-dependent processes with collapsing sample space |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=112 |issue=17 |pages=5348–5353 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1420946112 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=4418853 |pmid=25870294 |arxiv=1407.2775 |bibcode=2015PNAS..112.5348C }}</ref> He co-authored ''Introduction to the'' ''Theory of Complex Systems'' (2018) (together with Rudolf Hanel and Peter Klimek) that formalizes processes such as fragmentation, aggregation, and adaptive feedback, demonstrating how local interaction rules generate global patterns without centralized control – illustrated empirically by super-linear scaling in urban growth and linguistic evolution.<ref name=":2" />

=== Systemic Risk in Financial Networks ===
Thurner has studied systemic risk and contagion cascades in [[financial network]]s. A central contribution is the notion of the [[systemic risk]] transaction tax, a tax on the systemic risk of financial contracts, intended to reduce systemic risk in financial systems by rewiring financial networks. The efficacy of the systemic risk tax was shown in [[agent-based model]]s<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Thurner |first1=Stefan |last2=Poledna |first2=Sebastian |date=2013-05-28 |title=DebtRank-transparency: Controlling systemic risk in financial networks |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |page=1888 |doi=10.1038/srep01888  |doi-access=free|issn=2045-2322 |pmc=3664900 |pmid=23712454 |arxiv=1301.6115 |bibcode=2013NatSR...3.1888T }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/handbook-of-financial-stress-testing/4B5BE02A364329308DB7A7AE805E7572 |title=Handbook of Financial Stress Testing |date=2022 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-83073-7 |editor-last=Farmer |editor-first=J. Doyne |location=Cambridge |doi=10.1017/9781108903011 |editor-last2=Kleinnijenhuis |editor-first2=Alissa M. |editor-last3=Schuermann |editor-first3=Til |editor-last4=Wetzer |editor-first4=Thom}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Poledna |first1=Sebastian |last2=Thurner |first2=Stefan |date=2016-10-02 |title=Elimination of systemic risk in financial networks by means of a systemic risk transaction tax |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14697688.2016.1156146 |journal=Quantitative Finance |language=en |volume=16 |issue=10 |pages=1599–1613 |doi=10.1080/14697688.2016.1156146 |arxiv=1401.8026 |bibcode=2016QuFin..16.1599P |issn=1469-7688}}</ref> and in an equilibrium setting <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Leduc |first1=Matt V. |last2=Thurner |first2=Stefan |date=2017 |title=Incentivizing Resilience in Financial Networks |journal=SSRN Electronic Journal |doi=10.2139/ssrn.2794371 |ssrn=2794371 |issn=1556-5068}}</ref> of DebtRank, a nonlinear metric that quantifies systemic importance of firms, to financial contracts thus making it possible to estimate systemic risk of financial contracts. This opens the possibility to measure the systemic risk of financial contracts by assessing their capacity to distress other institutions beyond direct bilateral exposures.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Poledna |first1=Sebastian |last2=Molina-Borboa |first2=José Luis |last3=Martínez-Jaramillo |first3=Serafín |last4=van der Leij |first4=Marco |last5=Thurner |first5=Stefan |date=2015-10-01 |title=The multi-layer network nature of systemic risk and its implications for the costs of financial crises |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1572308915000856 |journal=Journal of Financial Stability |volume=20 |pages=70–81 |doi=10.1016/j.jfs.2015.08.001 |issn=1572-3089}}</ref> He extended the framework of systemic risk to multilayer financial networks encompassing loans, derivatives, and collateral. Related methods applied to firm-level [[supply chain]]s showed that rewiring supplier relationships toward lower-risk configurations measurably reduces disruption propagation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Diem |first1=Christian |last2=Borsos |first2=András |last3=Reisch |first3=Tobias |last4=Kertész |first4=János |last5=Thurner |first5=Stefan |date=2022-05-11 |title=Quantifying firm-level economic systemic risk from nation-wide supply networks |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=7719 |doi=10.1038/s41598-022-11522-z  |doi-access=free|issn=2045-2322 |pmc=9092945 |pmid=35546595 |arxiv=2104.07260 |bibcode=2022NatSR..12.7719D }}</ref>

=== Social Sciences ===
Thurner applies computational methods to [[social dynamics]], including [[Formation (group theory)|group formation]] and opinion [[attitude polarisation|polarization]]. A 2023 study used a spin-glass-inspired self-assembly framework to model how homophily drives the formation of social groups, deriving group-size distributions that match empirical data from online communities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Korbel |first1=Jan |last2=Lindner |first2=Simon D. |last3=Pham |first3=Tuan Minh |last4=Hanel |first4=Rudolf |last5=Thurner |first5=Stefan |date=2023-01-30 |title=Homophily-Based Social Group Formation in a Spin Glass Self-Assembly Framework |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.130.057401 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en |volume=130 |issue=5 |article-number=057401 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.130.057401 |pmid=36800470 |arxiv=2211.12210 |bibcode=2023PhRvL.130e7401K |issn=0031-9007}}</ref> A 2025 study demonstrated mathematically that increasing social connectivity can trigger sudden polarization once a critical societal connectivity threshold is exceeded, linking the rise in close friendships observed since 2000 to measured polarization trends in Western societies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Thurner |first1=Stefan |last2=Hofer |first2=Markus |last3=Korbel |first3=Jan |date=2025-11-04 |title=Why more social interactions lead to more polarization in societies |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=122 |issue=44 |article-number=e2517530122 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2517530122 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=12595431 |pmid=41171853}}</ref> Earlier work includes a 2010 PNAS study of social networks formed by more than 300,000 players in the massive multiplayer online game [[Pardus (video game)|Pardus]] including communication, trade, and conflict layers in an online social network, which uncovered gender-specific interaction patterns mirroring offline behavioral asymmetries.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Szell |first1=Michael |last2=Lambiotte |first2=Renaud |last3=Thurner |first3=Stefan |date=2010-08-03 |title=Multirelational organization of large-scale social networks in an online world |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=107 |issue=31 |pages=13636–13641 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1004008107 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=2922277 |pmid=20643965 |arxiv=1003.5137 |bibcode=2010PNAS..10713636S }}</ref>

== Reception and impact ==
Thurner has published over 300 peer-reviewed articles <ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Semantic Scholar |url=https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/S.-Thurner/1723195 |access-date=2026-03-06 |website=www.semanticscholar.org}}</ref> and holds three patents.<ref name=":0" /> His most cited contributions include foundational work on network dynamics, systemic risk, and social systems.<ref name=":3" />

Thurner has been active in communicating complexity science to non-specialist audiences. The Austrian Association of Education and Science Journalists elected him Scientist of the Year for 2017,<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":4" /> citing his sustained efforts to explain complexity research to the general public. The award, which has been given annually since 1994 and has previously been awarded to figures such as Anton Zeilinger and Josef Penninger, recognizes researchers for making their fields accessible to a broader public.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" />

In 2021, Thurner together with his former PhD student and colleague Peter Klimek received the Paul Watzlawick Ring of Honor from the Vienna Medical Association, in recognition of their work forecasting the course of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] using [[big data]] and advising the Austrian government during the crisis.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wien |first=Medizinischen Universität |title=Stefan Thurner und Peter Klimek erhalten Paul-Watzlawick-Ehrenring 2021 {{!}} MedUni Wien |url=https://www.meduniwien.ac.at//web/ueber-uns/news/news-im-april-2021/stefan-thurner-und-peter-klimek-erhalten-paul-watzlawick-ehrenring-2021/ |access-date=2026-03-06 |website=Medizinischen Universität Wien |language=de}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Paul-Watzlawick-Ehrenring für Stefan Thurner & Peter Klimek vom CSH Vienna |url=https://www.ots.at/presseaussendung/OTS_20211007_OTS0084/paul-watzlawick-ehrenring-fuer-stefan-thurner-peter-klimek-vom-csh-vienna |access-date=2026-03-06 |website=OTS.at |language=de}}</ref><ref name=":6" />

During the pandemic, Thurner partially redirected the Complexity Science Hub's research capacity to COVID-19-related questions, advising various bodies of the national government and communicating findings to the public.<ref name=":8" />

== Controversy ==

=== Interpretations of COVID-19 findings ===
In a 2020 paper, Thurner and colleagues attributed prolonged linear – rather than exponential – growth in COVID-19 case numbers across multiple countries to sparseness in contact networks, arguing that linear propagation under social-distancing conditions is possible and that standard SIR models, which assume homogeneous mixing, are ill-suited for early containment dynamics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Thurner |first1=Stefan |last2=Klimek |first2=Peter |last3=Hanel |first3=Rudolf |date=2020-09-15 |title=A network-based explanation of why most COVID-19 infection curves are linear |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=117 |issue=37 |pages=22684–22689 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2010398117 |doi-access=free |pmc=7502715 |pmid=32839315 |bibcode=2020PNAS..11722684T }}</ref> Critics Kuśmierz and Toyoizumi countered that linear growth on small-world networks arises only near the critical point (R ≈ 1) and questioned whether the observed patterns require the specific network topology proposed.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kuśmierz |first1=Łukasz |last2=Toyoizumi |first2=Taro |title=Infection curves on small-world networks are linear only in the vicinity of the critical point |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=2021 |volume=118 |issue=10 |article-number=e2024297118 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2024297118 |doi-access=free |pmc=7958250 |pmid=33637610 |bibcode=2021PNAS..11824297K }}</ref> Thurner and co-authors replied that their model explicitly concerns the near-critical regime and characterized the criticism as a misreading of the paper's scope.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Thurner |first1=Stefan |last2=Klimek |first2=Peter |last3=Hanel |first3=Rudolf |title=Reply to Kuśmierz and Toyoizumi: A network-based explanation of why most COVID-19 infection curves are linear |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=2021 |volume=118 |issue=10 |article-number=e2100906118 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2100906118 |doi-access=free |pmc=7958403 |pmid=33637611 |bibcode=2021PNAS..11800906T }}</ref>

== Selected publications ==

=== Books ===

*2020: S. Thurner: ''Die Zerbrechlichkeit der Welt. Kollaps oder Wende. Wir haben es in der Hand'', [https://www.edition-a.at/buecher/wirtschaft/19/die-zerbrechlichkeit-der-welt edition a], Wien 2020, {{ISBN|978-3-99001-428-8}}
*2018: S. Thurner, R. Hanel, P. Klimek: ''Introduction to the Theory of Complex Systems'', [[Oxford University Press]], Oxford 2018, {{ISBN|9780198821939}}
* 2012: S. Thurner, H. Meyer-Ortmanns: ''Principles of evolution: from the Planck epoch to complex multicellular life.'' Springer, Berlin/ Heidelberg 2011, {{ISBN|978-3-642-26802-1}}
*2012: S. Thurner: ''Systemic financial risk'', Steinbeis/OECD Publishing, Stuttgart/ Paris, {{ISBN|978-3-941417-93-9}}
